Open

This deck explains one idea: what a digital worker is, and what this particular one does. It is a concept explainer, not a product tour.

The thesis to land

A digital worker is a role with skills, not a chatbot. This one sits at the point where a job closes — the only place where maintenance data can still be fixed.

Logistics

Seven slides. Three of them are interactive — hover the diagram, don't read the labels out. The big one is next-but-one.

The idea

A digital worker is a role, not a robot

You hire it for a job, you give it skills, and you set the rules it works to. Same as a new starter.

The job
It owns one piece of work
This one reviews a finished maintenance task before it closes. That is the whole job description.
The skills
Each skill does one thing
A skill is a single capability you can add, change or take away. You train it the way you would train a person.
The rules
It works from evidence only
It uses what is on the record. When the information is not there, it stops and asks rather than filling in the gap.
The shift. You are not automating a screen. You are adding a colleague who does the same review on every job, every shift, and never gets tired at line two hundred.

02 / 07

Headline

Get the mental model right before showing anything. Job, skills, rules — three words.

Walk the cards

The job — narrow on purpose. A digital worker that does everything does nothing well.
The skills — this is the bit people underestimate. Skills are modular; you can add a fifth tomorrow.
The rules — the trust card. Say it plainly: it does not invent. Anticipate the hallucination question here and defuse it early.

Bridge

"So that is the shape of the thing. Let me show you the one we built."

The digital worker

One worker in the middle, four skills around it

Hover a skill
IFSDigital Worker
03 / 07

This is the slide

Everything else supports this one. Stay on it. Let the diagram breathe before you touch it.

Drive it

Start on the centre — the worker itself — then hover each skill in turn, clockwise from top-left. The panel on the right explains each one. Do not read the panel aloud. Let them read; you add the one line the panel does not say.

The lines to add per skill

Checking the write-up — "it will not write the note for the technician. It asks them."
Catching leftover work — "the second fault the tech found stops disappearing into free text."
Spotting repeat problems — "'third time this year' is a reliability finding. Today nobody reads it."
Signing off the time — "this is the only one it decides on its own, and only inside a band you set."

Bridge

"Four skills. They do not fire at random — there is an order, and the order is the point."

How it runs

Each skill is a gate, and they run in order

Nothing gets signed off until everything before it has been looked at. Anything unclear stops the run and goes to a person.

Hover a gate

04 / 07

Headline

The order is a design decision, not an implementation detail. Sign-off is last, deliberately — you do not want hours authorised on a job whose write-up nobody could understand.

Drive it

Trace left to right with the cursor. Then hover the drop-out arrow underneath: that is the exit that matters. Anything it is unsure about leaves the pipeline and lands with a human, with the reason attached.

Honesty point

"It stops far more often than people expect. That is the feature."

The output

One finished job, four things that would not otherwise exist

Hover an outcome
IFSDigital Worker
05 / 07

Headline

This is the value slide. One routine job goes in. Four usable things come out — and today three of them do not exist at all.

Drive it

Start at the left: one closeout note, written at ten to six, at the asset. Then fan right. Land on the last one — the improvement — because that is the one nobody currently gets.

Bridge

"Which raises the obvious question — how much of this is it deciding on its own?"

The guardrails

It drafts. A person decides.

The limits are built in, not configured in. This is what it will never do.

It never closes the job
It cannot change the status of a work task. The record is handed back to you exactly where it was.
It never invents detail
If a fact is not on the record, it does not appear in the output. No assumed cause, no assumed severity.
It never creates without a confirm
Follow-up work and improvements are drafted for review. A person clicks before anything is raised.
It never hides its working
Every decision comes back with what it looked at and why it landed where it did.
Only one call is its own. Signing off hours that fall inside a tolerance you set. Everything else is a recommendation with a person on the end of it.
IFSDigital Worker
06 / 07

Headline

Answer the fear before it is asked out loud. Four "nevers", then the single exception stated plainly.

Tone

Flat and factual. No selling here. This slide earns the right to everything else.

If challenged on autonomy

"It makes one decision on its own, inside a band you configure. Everything else it drafts and a person confirms. It cannot close a work order — that authority was never given to it."

IN ONE LINE

Bad maintenance data
is fixed at the moment
it is written

Not in a dashboard, not in a data cleanse, not in an audit six months later. At the asset, at ten to six, in the box where somebody types "done".

›  A role with four skills
›  Same check on every job
›  Drafts, never decides for you
IFSDigital Worker
07 / 07

Land it

Slow down. This is the sentence you want repeated in the room after you leave.

The argument

Every maintenance organisation tries to fix data quality at the reporting end. You cannot clean your way out of it — the data is bad at the moment of creation. That is the only place it can be fixed, and that is where this sits.

Close

Pause. Then hand over, or go to questions. Do not add a summary after this.
